analysis.one_liner: Boosts bankruptcy protections for laid-off workers and retirees while capping executive bonuses in bankrupt companies.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in the final weeks of the 118th Congress, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company files for bankruptcy, workers owed wages and severance, retirees counting on pensions and health benefits, and unions with contracts often rank behind lenders, while company executives can keep collecting bonuses and retention pay. This bill would flip part of that balance: it doubles the amount of unpaid wages that get paid first, protects severance and retiree benefits, makes it much harder to tear up union contracts, lets courts favor buyers who keep jobs and pensions, and restricts, claws back, or blocks executive bonuses and golden parachutes in bankrupt companies. It never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees of companies that go bankrupt: they would collect more of their unpaid wages, severance, and benefit contributions before other creditors are paid; retirees would keep stronger protection for health and pension benefits; union members would keep their contracts unless the company proves in court that cuts are truly necessary; and 401(k) participants could claim losses where the employer committed fraud. Rank-and-file employees would also gain from new limits on executive bonuses, retention pay, and golden parachutes in bankruptcy, including clawbacks when pensions are dumped on the federal pension insurer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority cap on unpaid wages from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker and removes the 180-day look-back limit, so more back pay is paid ahead of other creditors when a company goes under.

Makes severance pay and unpaid employer contributions to benefit plans payable administrative expenses, and lets laid-off workers claim damages under the WARN Act (the law requiring advance notice of mass layoffs) with priority.

Requires a bankruptcy plan to continue retiree health benefits unless the company meets a strict court test, and gives workers and retirees their own claims for pension shortfalls and for losses in company stock held in 401(k)-type plans when the employer committed fraud or breached a duty.

Rewrites the rules for rejecting union contracts: the company must negotiate in good faith first, can only seek the minimum savings essential to exit bankruptcy, must include management cost cuts in any savings program, and a court can approve rejection only on 'clear and convincing' evidence — with a presumption against rejection if the company paid executive bonuses.

Bars most bonuses and incentive pay for insiders, senior executives, top-20 earners, division managers, and consultants in bankruptcy, caps exit pay at the 50th percentile of comparable industry compensation, and creates a clawback to recover a share of executive compensation proportional to any cut imposed on pensions or retiree benefits.
Requires bankruptcy courts weighing asset sales to give substantial weight to whichever buyer preserves jobs, maintains pay and conditions, and assumes pension and retiree health obligations.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors of failed companies — particularly secured lenders and distressed-debt investors — would recover less, since a larger share of the estate would go to unpaid wages, severance, benefits, and pension claims. Executives, top-20 earners, division managers, and consultants at bankrupt companies would lose access to bonuses, retention pay, and large exit packages, and could face clawbacks. Companies could also face somewhat higher costs of borrowing, since lenders would bear more of the loss in a bankruptcy.
analysis.who_pays_short: Secured lenders, distressed investors, and bankruptcy executives

drawbacks.text: Doubling the wage priority to $20,000 per worker and making unpaid severance and benefit contributions a cost charged against lenders' collateral means creditors recover less when a company fails — which can make lenders charge more, or refuse to lend, to struggling companies that employ many people.

The bill makes it substantially harder to cut labor costs in bankruptcy: union contracts can be changed only after good-faith bargaining under a 'clear and convincing' standard, and management incentive pay is sharply restricted — restrictions that restructuring specialists argue can hamper turnarounds and, in some cases, push a failing firm into liquidation, destroying the jobs the bill aims to save.

Requiring courts to favor buyers who preserve jobs and match pension and health obligations could steer asset sales toward lower bids, reducing recoveries for creditors — a cost that can flow back to lenders, pension funds, and other investors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and concrete: doubled wage priority, protection for severance, retiree health, pensions, and union contracts, and clawbacks of executive pay in failing companies. The costs are also real and fall on credit and capital: creditors recover less when a company fails, which makes lending to struggling, labor-heavy businesses more expensive, and the strict new standards for cutting union contracts or retiree benefits — plus limits on management incentive pay — could make turnarounds harder in some cases and push some firms toward liquidation rather than reorganization. The bill could have benefited from testing these trade-offs in hearings and markups; it received none.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last month of the 118th Congress and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired with the Congress on January 3, 2025 without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2024, less than a month before the 118th Congress ended.
Its only action beyond introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, all bills not passed by both chambers expire, so the bill died with no vote ever taken in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of bankrupt companies, secured lenders, and distressed-credit investors keep the current bankruptcy rules, under which unpaid wages and benefits rank behind other creditors and executive bonuses and retention pay generally survive reorganization.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bankruptcy executives, secured lenders, distressed-credit investors

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic lead sponsor, 7 additional Democratic cosponsors, and 1 Republican (Sen. Hawley) among its 9 cosponsors — and no member of either party is recorded opposing it, because it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill subordinates their claims: unpaid wages up to $20,000 per worker, severance, benefit contributions, and WARN Act damages would be paid out of the estate and charged against their collateral, leaving them with smaller recoveries when a company fails.

industries.industry: Executives and consultants of failing companies
industries.note: Bonus and incentive pay programs would be barred or sharply capped, exit compensation limited to the industry median, deferred compensation forfeited in some cases, and clawback claims created where executives were paid while pensions or retiree benefits were cut.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy restructuring professionals and the insolvency bar
industries.note: More contested hearings, claims, and clawback litigation would mean more work, but companies and creditors would have less money to pay for it, and fee and bonus pools would shrink.
Their workers would be far better protected if they fail, but the higher cost of bankruptcy for their lenders could make credit more expensive or harder to obtain before that point.
